title: Loveless
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: Ritsuka Aoyagi, a 12-year-old with no memory of his life before age ten, is berated and physically abused by his mother, and his protective older brother Seimei has apparently been killed. Soubi, an adult art student who says he was Seimei's friend, tells Ritsuka his true name is 'Loveless' and draws him into a secret world where paired 'Fighters' and 'Sacrifices' duel with spoken spells. Ritsuka searches for the truth about his brother and for acceptance of who he is now.
life_message: Being accepted as the person you are, and choosing bonds freely rather than having them imposed, is what makes love real.

content.note: Spell duels that wound the Sacrifice; branding, blood and knife attacks; mother beats Ritsuka (AniList blurb; Manga Bookshelf).
Heavy, melancholy mystery; a volume-five abuse scene called 'incredibly disturbing' (Manga Bookshelf).
Romantic undertones between adult Soubi and 12-year-old Ritsuka kept short of explicit; Soubi's past sexual abuse; an ordered rape; incest theme (review; AniList Rape, Incest tags; Viz).
Child abuse by a parent, amnesia and identity loss, bullying (AniList tags; MangaDex; review).
Dominant/submissive 'Sacrifice-Fighter' bond and adult-child closeness presented as romantic (Viz 'pseudo-BDSM'; review calls it uncomfortable).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Wounds and insults are settled by spell duels between pairs.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Bonds are assigned by a hidden organization; Ritsuka seeks to choose his own.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Brotherly loyalty to Seimei and the paired bond drive Ritsuka's choices.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Sacrifice commands, Fighter obeys; Ritsuka questions this ranking.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Secret school and spells, but identity is reasoned out personally.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Acceptance of oneself and complex, ambiguous loves are the story's focus.

folkways.japan: The cat-ear (kemonomimi) character design and the sixth-grade school setting follow Japanese manga conventions; keeping family troubles private is a common Japanese norm that frames the mother's abuse, described here as context (to verify).

delivery.evidence: Manga Bookshelf reviewers say Kouga avoids 'flashing arrows' explaining her themes and does not vilify flawed adults.
delivery.note: Themes of love and control emerge through character relationships rather than stated lessons.

winners_losers: Ritsuka's search for selfhood and for chosen loyalty gets the story's sympathy; controlling figures such as Seimei and the abusive mother are shown causing lasting harm. Reviewers note that flawed adults are not simply vilified.
to_verify: Soubi's exact age and how far the adult-child romantic dynamic goes in later volumes; reviewers say it stays short of explicit.
